title: Broadcasting, axes and mutation order
outcome: Use broadcasting with explicit axes and distinguish an elementwise formula from a mutation-order-dependent algorithm.
key_terms: Applying a function elementwise across arrays and scalars, expanding singleton dimensions so compatible shapes combine.
Writing `f.(x)` or `x .+ y` requests broadcasting, and the `@.` macro adds a dot to every call in an expression.
Nested dotted calls in one expression combine into a single loop without allocating temporary arrays.
An axis of length one that broadcasting repeats to match the other operand, so a column and a row form a matrix.
When a loop writes values that later iterations read, such as a shift, the result depends on write order unless the source is snapshotted.
approach: Write the indexed formula first, then make array axes express it. Broadcasting extends singleton axes and fails when lengths disagree. The worked example adds per-row offsets `[10, 20]` and a one-row array of per-column offsets. For in-place loops, ask whether a read sees earlier writes, since that decides recurrence or snapshot behavior.

exercises.title: Choose the axis
exercises.task: Add one offset per column to a matrix.
exercises.expected: Reshape the offsets into a one-row array.
exercises.answer: The explicit singleton axis documents the intended broadcast alignment.
exercises.why: `reshape([100, 200, 300], 1, 3)` has size `(1, 3)`, so it lines up with the three columns of `[1 3 5; 2 4 6]`.
exercises.wrong: Adding the plain vector `[100, 200, 300]` tries to match it with the two rows and raises `DimensionMismatch`.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts the result `[111 213 315; 122 224 326]`; the reference checks `size(reshape([1, 2, 3], 1, 3)) == (1, 3)`.

exercises.title: Reject incompatible axes
exercises.task: Broadcast a length 4 vector with the 2-by-3 fixture.
exercises.hint: Compatible axes are not determined by total element count.
exercises.answer: Shape validation prevents a silent interpretation of an unintended operation.
exercises.why: A length 4 vector aligns with the first axis of length 2, which is neither equal nor 1, so broadcasting throws.
exercises.wrong: Arguing that 4 elements fit somewhere in a 6-element matrix treats total size as the rule rather than per-axis compatibility.

exercises.title: Update in place
exercises.task: Apply 2x+1 elementwise to a floating vector using dotted assignment.
exercises.expected: The destination values change to the expected affine result.
exercises.hint: Each output depends only on the corresponding old element.
exercises.answer: This dependence pattern makes the specific self-update straightforward to reason about.
exercises.why: `values .= 2 .* values .+ 1` fuses into one loop where each output reads only its own old element, so `[1, 2, 3]` becomes `[3, 5, 7]`.
exercises.wrong: Writing `values = 2 .* values .+ 1` allocates a new array and rebinds the name, so other references to the original see no change.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `values == [3, 5, 7]`; the reference checks a similar dotted assignment giving `[0.5, 1.0]`.

exercises.title: Trace a manual recurrence
exercises.task: Shift a vector left-to-right by reading the preceding updated element.
exercises.hint: A later read sees an earlier write.
exercises.answer: The loop implements a recurrence, not a simultaneous snapshot assignment.
exercises.why: In the loop `sequential[i] = sequential[i-1]`, position 2 receives 1, and position 3 then reads that new 1, so all four entries become 1.
exercises.wrong: Expecting a shift to `[1, 1, 2, 3]` assumes each read sees the original values, which only holds with separate source storage.

exercises.title: Preserve a snapshot
exercises.task: Read the shift input from an explicit copy.
exercises.answer: The copy changes the read/write dependency and therefore the algorithm.
exercises.why: Reading from `source = copy(snapshot)` keeps the old values available, so the shift gives `[1, 1, 2, 3]`.
exercises.wrong: Taking a `view` of the array instead of a copy shares storage and reproduces the recurrence result.

exercises.title: Choose a destination type
exercises.task: Write 0.5 into an integer element through dotted assignment.
exercises.hint: Mutation does not make the destination representation arbitrary.
exercises.answer: Allocate a representation that can express the intended result.
exercises.why: `Int[0] .= [0.5]` must convert 0.5 into the existing `Int` element, which is inexact, so `InexactError` is raised.
exercises.wrong: Expecting the destination to widen to `Float64` misunderstands in-place assignment, which never changes the element type of an existing array.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `@test_throws InexactError Int[0] .= [0.5]`; allocate `zeros(1)` when fractional results are expected.

checks_note: Broadcasting rules appear one at a time: `sin.` applies elementwise, a scalar expands across `[1, 2]`, and `.*` multiplies matching positions rather than performing a matrix product. `reshape` turns three values into a one by three row without copying them. The `destination .=` line writes into existing storage, and the final `InexactError` shows that an in-place write into `Int` storage cannot hold 0.5.
